title: Pollution, Climate and Sustainability
bigQuestion: How does a society find out that something invisible is harming it, prove it, and then decide what to do at a cost it is willing to pay?

story.title: The Hole in the Sky
story.kicker: Three British scientists at a frozen outpost found that a layer protecting all life on Earth was thinning, and the world did something rare: it agreed to fix it.
paragraphs: Halley Bay is a research station on the Antarctic coast, built on floating ice. Since 1957 scientists there had pointed an instrument called a Dobson spectrophotometer at the sky each spring to measure ozone, a form of oxygen with three atoms per molecule instead of two. High in the stratosphere, ozone absorbs most of the sun's harmful ultraviolet light. Without it, skin cancers and cataracts would soar and plankton at the base of the ocean food chain would suffer. The readings had held steady for years at around 300 Dobson units.

In the early 1980s, Joseph Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jonathan Shanklin noticed the October numbers dropping. At first they suspected the aging instrument, so they checked it against a new one. The drop was real. By 1984 the spring ozone over Halley Bay had fallen by roughly a third. They published the finding in the journal Nature in May 1985. A satellite had been recording ozone the whole time, but its software had been set to flag readings that low as errors. Once NASA rechecked the raw data, the satellite confirmed it: a hole the size of a continent, opening every spring.

The cause was already on the table. In 1974, chemists Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland had published a warning that chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, the stable, nontoxic gases used in spray cans, refrigerators and air conditioners, would drift up to the stratosphere, be broken apart by ultraviolet light, and release chlorine atoms that destroy ozone. One chlorine atom could wreck thousands of ozone molecules before it was removed. Industry called the idea speculative. The Antarctic measurements made it hard to keep saying so, and in 1987 expeditions flew into the hole and measured high chlorine right where ozone was lowest.

That same year, nations signed the Montreal Protocol, agreeing to cut CFC production, and later to phase it out entirely. Chemists found substitutes. Every country on Earth eventually joined. Molina, Rowland and Paul Crutzen shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1995. The ozone hole still opens each spring, because CFCs linger for decades, but it has stopped growing and is expected to recover around the middle of this century. It is the clearest case we have of the pattern this chapter is about: a measurement, a mechanism, a hard argument, and a decision.
story.think: The satellite saw the ozone hole before the scientists at Halley Bay did, but its software threw the data out as impossible. What does that say about the risk of assuming you already know what the answer should look like?

lessons.title: When Air Became a Problem
lessons.mainIdea: Deadly smog episodes and steady measurement forced the United States to set enforceable limits on air pollution, and the air has grown much cleaner since.
reading: In late October 1948, a temperature inversion, a layer of warm air sitting on top of cold air, trapped the smoke from steel and zinc works over the town of Donora, Pennsylvania. For five days the fog was so thick that people could not see across the street. About twenty people died and thousands fell ill. Four years later, in December 1952, a similar inversion held coal smoke over London, and the death toll ran into the thousands. Air pollution stopped being a nuisance and became, in the public mind, something that could kill.

The pollutants have names and sources. *Particulate matter*, tiny solid and liquid specks, comes from combustion, dust and smoke and lodges deep in the lungs. Sulfur dioxide comes mostly from burning coal and makes acid rain. Nitrogen oxides from car engines and power plants react in sunlight with vapors from fuel and solvents to form ground-level ozone, the main ingredient of *smog*, which irritates lungs and damages crops. Carbon monoxide from incomplete burning blocks blood from carrying oxygen. Lead, once added to gasoline, damages children's brains. Each of these was once simply released into the air.

The Clean Air Act of 1970 changed that. It directed the new Environmental Protection Agency to set national standards for these common pollutants based on health, and required states, including Illinois, to write plans to meet them. Later amendments removed lead from gasoline, required catalytic converters on cars and, in 1990, created a market for sulfur dioxide permits to cut acid rain. The results are measurable. The EPA reports that combined emissions of the main regulated pollutants fell by roughly three-quarters between 1970 and the 2020s, while the economy, population and miles driven all grew. Blood lead levels in American children dropped by more than 90 percent.

Chicago's air is far cleaner than it was in the 1960s, when steel mills lined the Calumet region and soot blackened buildings. It still fails the ozone standard on hot summer days, and neighborhoods near highways, rail yards and remaining industry breathe more particulate matter than others. Clean air is not a finished job. It is an ongoing measurement, with a standard to compare against and a law that requires the gap to close.

words.d: tiny solid or liquid particles suspended in air, from smoke, dust and exhaust, that can lodge deep in the lungs
hazy, irritating air pollution, especially ground-level ozone formed when vehicle and industrial emissions react in sunlight
a layer of warm air above cooler air near the ground that traps pollution close to the surface
the 1970 U.S. law, amended since, that sets national health-based limits on common air pollutants

look.title: What the Law Is For
look.text: The Clean Air Act states its first purpose as protecting and improving the quality of the nation's air resources in order to promote public health and welfare and the productive capacity of the population.
look.cite: Clean Air Act, Section 101(b)(1), United States Code Title 42, Section 7401 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: The law names health, welfare and productive capacity together. Why might Congress have listed the economy alongside health rather than treating them as opposites?

check.q: What weather condition trapped deadly pollution over Donora in 1948 and London in 1952?
choices: A hurricane
A temperature inversion holding cold air under warm air
A heat wave with strong winds
A blizzard
check.why: Warm air above cold air stops the vertical mixing that normally carries smoke away, so pollution builds up near the ground.

check.q: Ground-level ozone smog forms mainly when
choices: nitrogen oxides and fuel vapors react in sunlight
coal is burned on cold nights
the stratospheric ozone layer sinks
lead is added to gasoline
check.why: Sunlight drives reactions between nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, producing ozone near the ground.

check.q: Which statement about U.S. air since 1970 is supported by EPA measurements?
choices: Air pollution has doubled with population growth
Emissions fell only because the economy shrank
Emissions of the main regulated pollutants fell by roughly three-quarters while the economy grew
Lead in children's blood has stayed the same
check.why: EPA data show large emission declines under the Clean Air Act even as population, economic output and driving all increased.

lessons.title: Rivers That Caught Fire
lessons.mainIdea: Water pollution comes from pipes you can point to and from land you cannot, and the law has been far more successful with the first than the second.
reading: On June 22, 1969, oil and debris floating on the Cuyahoga River in Cleveland caught fire. The river had burned before, more than a dozen times, but this time the story spread nationwide and became a symbol. Lake Erie, which the Cuyahoga feeds, was choked with algae and its fish were dying. In Chicago, the river had been so foul from stockyards and sewage that in 1900 engineers reversed its flow. A new canal sent the city's waste toward the Illinois River and the Mississippi instead of into Lake Michigan, the drinking water supply.

Congress passed the Clean Water Act in 1972. Its most powerful tool was simple: no one may discharge pollution from a pipe into a river or lake without a permit that limits what and how much. Pollution that comes out of an identifiable pipe or ditch is called *point source* pollution. Factories and sewage plants are point sources. The law also paid for thousands of modern sewage treatment plants. The results were dramatic. Fish returned to rivers that had been open sewers, and the Cuyahoga now hosts kayakers and restaurants along its banks.

The other kind of pollution was left largely alone. *Nonpoint source* pollution comes from everywhere at once: fertilizer and manure washing off fields, oil and salt off streets, sediment from construction sites, bacteria from failing septic tanks. There is no pipe to put a permit on. Today, nonpoint runoff, mostly from agriculture, is the leading reason U.S. rivers and lakes fail water quality standards, and it is the source of the nitrogen that builds the Gulf dead zone. Illinois rivers such as the Illinois and the Kaskaskia carry it in every spring rain.

Drinking water is regulated separately, under the Safe Drinking Water Act of 1974, which sets limits for contaminants at the tap. Nitrate is one of them, because at high levels it can interfere with oxygen in infants' blood. Some Illinois and Iowa towns that draw from rivers or shallow wells in farm country must treat their water or blend it to stay under the nitrate limit. The pollutant that leaves a field as a farm problem arrives in town as a public health bill.

words.d: pollution that enters water from a single identifiable place, such as a pipe or ditch
pollution that washes into water from a wide area, such as runoff from fields, streets and lawns
the 1972 U.S. law that requires permits for discharging pollution into rivers and lakes and funded sewage treatment
soil and rock particles carried by water that cloud streams and smother habitat when they settle

look.title: Two Sources, One Creek
look.text: A creek runs past a small cheese factory with a single outfall pipe and then along five miles of farm fields and a subdivision of lawns. A state inspector samples the water. Just below the pipe, phosphorus is high. Five miles downstream, after a rainstorm, phosphorus and nitrate are far higher still, and the water is brown with sediment. The factory has a permit and is within its limits.
look.prompt: Which source is easier to regulate, and why? What kinds of tools might reduce the second source when a permit cannot?

check.q: Why did engineers reverse the Chicago River in 1900?
choices: To power mills
To create a shipping shortcut to Canada
To drain the prairie for farming
To keep the city's sewage out of its Lake Michigan drinking water
check.why: Reversing the flow sent waste down a canal toward the Illinois River instead of into the lake the city drank from.

check.q: Which is an example of nonpoint source pollution?
choices: Fertilizer washing off many farm fields in a rainstorm
A factory outfall pipe
A sewage treatment plant's discharge
A leaking oil tanker
check.why: Nonpoint pollution comes from a broad area with no single pipe, which is why permits cannot easily control it.

check.q: Why has the Clean Water Act been more effective against factories than against farms?
choices: Farms are exempt from all environmental laws
Factories produce less pollution
Its permit system works on identifiable pipes, which farms mostly do not have
Farm runoff is not harmful
check.why: The law's core tool is the discharge permit, which fits point sources but not diffuse runoff from fields.

lessons.title: The Ozone Fix
lessons.mainIdea: The recovery of the ozone layer shows what it takes to solve a global environmental problem: a clear mechanism, a measurable trend, available substitutes and an agreement with teeth.
reading: The ozone story has a beginning, a middle and, unusually, an ending in sight. The beginning was chemistry. Molina and Rowland worked out on paper in 1974 that CFCs, which are so stable that nothing in the lower atmosphere breaks them down, would eventually reach the *stratosphere*, 15 to 50 kilometers up, where hard ultraviolet light could split them and free chlorine. A chlorine atom takes an oxygen atom from ozone, then gives it up again and repeats. It is a *catalyst*, unchanged by the reaction, so one atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules over its stay.

The middle was measurement and argument. Halley Bay's readings and the satellite data showed the hole. The 1987 aircraft flights into it found chlorine monoxide, the smoking gun of the chlorine reaction, rising exactly where ozone fell. Why Antarctica? Its winter is so cold that clouds of ice form in the stratosphere, and on their surfaces chlorine is converted into its most destructive forms, ready to attack when spring sunlight returns. The chemistry explained not just that ozone was falling but where and when, and a prediction that fits the details is far more convincing than one that fits only the headline.

The end was policy. The Montreal Protocol of 1987, strengthened several times since, set a schedule to phase out CFCs and related chemicals. Three things made it work. Substitutes were available or soon developed, so the cost was manageable. Wealthier nations helped pay for poorer nations to switch. And the agreement had a mechanism to tighten controls as the science firmed up. Chlorine in the stratosphere peaked in the late 1990s and has been falling since. Scientific assessments project the Antarctic ozone layer will return to its 1980 condition around the 2060s.

The fix had a side effect worth knowing: CFCs are also powerful *greenhouse gases*, so the protocol did more to slow warming than any climate treaty of its era. The main replacements, HFCs, do not harm ozone but do trap heat, and a 2016 amendment now phases those down too. Ozone was in some ways an easy case: a few chemicals, a few hundred companies, clear substitutes. Climate change involves the fuels that run everything. But the shape of the solution is the same, and the ozone layer is proof the shape can work.

words.d: the layer of the atmosphere from about 15 to 50 kilometers up, where the ozone layer lies
a substance that speeds a chemical reaction without being used up, so it can act again and again
chlorofluorocarbon, a stable manufactured gas once used in refrigerators and spray cans that destroys stratospheric ozone
the 1987 international agreement, joined by every nation, to phase out ozone-destroying chemicals
a gas such as carbon dioxide, methane or a CFC that absorbs heat radiating from Earth and warms the atmosphere

look.title: A Warning Before the Hole
look.text: In their 1974 paper, Molina and Rowland argued that chlorofluorocarbons released at the ground would survive for decades and slowly rise into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light would break them apart and release chlorine atoms, and that those atoms would catalytically destroy ozone in a chain of reactions, threatening the layer that shields the surface from ultraviolet radiation.
look.cite: Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland, Nature, 1974 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: This prediction came eleven years before the ozone hole was reported. What does it mean for a scientific claim when a later measurement matches a prediction made in advance?

check.q: Why can a single chlorine atom destroy thousands of ozone molecules?
choices: It acts as a catalyst and is not used up in the reaction
It splits into many chlorine atoms
It absorbs ultraviolet light
It combines permanently with ozone
check.why: Chlorine takes an oxygen atom from ozone, releases it, and repeats the cycle without being consumed.

check.q: Why does the ozone hole form over Antarctica in spring?
choices: CFCs are used most in the southern hemisphere
Extreme cold forms stratospheric ice clouds that prepare chlorine to attack when sunlight returns
Antarctica has no ozone to begin with
Volcanoes there release chlorine
check.why: Polar stratospheric clouds convert chlorine into active forms during the dark winter, and spring sunlight triggers rapid ozone loss.

check.q: Which factor was most important in making the Montreal Protocol succeed?
choices: CFCs were only used in one country
The ozone hole closed by itself
Substitutes were available and the agreement could tighten as evidence grew
Refrigerators were banned worldwide
check.why: Affordable replacements, help for poorer nations and a mechanism to strengthen the rules let the world phase out CFCs.

lessons.title: The Greenhouse Effect
lessons.mainIdea: Certain gases in the air let sunlight in but slow heat from escaping, and adding more of them warms the planet; this physics has been measured since the 1800s.
reading: Earth is warmer than it should be. A bare rock at our distance from the sun would average about minus 18 degrees Celsius, well below freezing. The actual average is about 15 degrees. The difference is the *greenhouse effect*. Sunlight, mostly visible, passes through the air and warms the ground. The warm ground gives off infrared radiation, heat you cannot see. Nitrogen and oxygen, which make up 99 percent of the air, let infrared pass straight through. But water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane and a few other gases absorb it and radiate part of it back down. They act like a blanket, not a mirror.

This is not new science. In 1859 the Irish physicist John Tyndall built an apparatus that passed heat radiation through tubes of different gases and measured how much got through. Nitrogen and oxygen absorbed almost nothing; water vapor and carbon dioxide absorbed strongly. In 1896 the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius, working with pencil and paper for a year, calculated that doubling the carbon dioxide in the air would warm the planet by several degrees. His number was rough, but his reasoning stands, and the effect he described has since been confirmed by laboratory spectroscopy, by satellites that measure infrared leaving Earth, and by instruments on the ground that measure infrared coming back down.

The gas that matters most in the long run is carbon dioxide, because it lasts centuries in the air and because we add so much of it. In 1958 Charles David Keeling began measuring it precisely at an observatory on Mauna Loa in Hawaii, high above local pollution. His record, now called the Keeling curve, shows a sawtooth line. It dips each northern summer as plants grow and rises each winter, a planet breathing. Underneath the sawtooth, the line climbs relentlessly, from about 315 parts per million in 1958 to over 420 today. Air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice show that before the industrial era it was about 280. In the past 800,000 years it never rose above about 300.

How do we know the extra carbon dioxide comes from fossil fuels and not from volcanoes or the ocean? Fossil carbon has a chemical signature: it contains almost no carbon-14, a radioactive form that decays away over thousands of years, and it is slightly depleted in carbon-13 compared with air. As fossil fuel carbon has flooded the atmosphere, both signatures have shifted exactly as expected. The ocean, meanwhile, is gaining carbon dioxide and turning slightly more acidic, so it cannot be the source. The bookkeeping closes.

words.d: the warming of Earth's surface caused by gases that absorb infrared heat radiating from the ground and send part of it back down
invisible heat radiation given off by warm objects, including Earth's surface
the continuous record of atmospheric carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since 1958
a unit of concentration; 420 parts per million means 420 molecules of a gas in every million molecules of air

look.title: Carbon Dioxide in the Air
rows: Ice age low, about 20,000 years ago
look.cite: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory and Antarctic ice-core records, rounded
look.prompt: How much did carbon dioxide rise between 1959 and 2020, and how does that compare with the total change from the ice age low to pre-industrial times, which took thousands of years?

check.q: Which gases are mainly responsible for the natural greenhouse effect?
choices: Nitrogen and oxygen
Water vapor and carbon dioxide
Argon and helium
Ozone and chlorine
check.why: Tyndall showed that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb infrared heat strongly while nitrogen and oxygen let it pass.

check.q: What does the yearly sawtooth in the Keeling curve show?
choices: Volcanic eruptions each spring
Errors in the instrument
Plants in the northern hemisphere taking up carbon dioxide in summer and releasing it in winter
Ocean tides
check.why: The seasonal dip and rise track the growth and decay of land plants, mostly in the northern hemisphere where most land lies.

check.q: What evidence shows that the added carbon dioxide comes from fossil fuels rather than volcanoes or the ocean?
choices: Volcanoes have stopped erupting
The ocean is losing carbon dioxide
Carbon dioxide only comes from burning
The air's carbon has shifted toward fossil carbon's signature, and the ocean is gaining carbon dioxide, not losing it
check.why: Fossil carbon lacks carbon-14 and is low in carbon-13; the atmosphere's isotopes have shifted accordingly, and the ocean is a sink, not a source.

lessons.title: Lines of Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Warming is documented by many independent records, from thermometers to ice cores to sea level, that all point the same direction.
reading: A claim this large should not rest on one measurement, and it does not. Thermometer records from thousands of weather stations, ships and buoys, kept since the 1880s and analyzed separately by NASA, NOAA, the UK Met Office and others, show that Earth's average surface temperature has risen a little over 1 degree Celsius since the late 1800s, with most of the rise since 1970. The groups use different methods and reach the same curve. The warmest years on record have nearly all come in the last decade.

Nature keeps its own records. Ice cores drilled from Greenland and Antarctica hold layers of snow going back hundreds of thousands of years, with air bubbles that preserve ancient atmosphere and chemical signatures that reveal past temperature. They show carbon dioxide and temperature rising and falling together through the ice ages. Tree rings, corals and lake sediments fill in the last few thousand years. Glaciers photographed a century ago have retreated up their valleys. Arctic sea ice at the end of summer, measured by satellite since 1979, has shrunk by roughly 40 percent in area. Spring arrives earlier; birds and plants have shifted their ranges north.

The ocean is the biggest thermometer of all. It stores more than 90 percent of the extra heat, and a fleet of thousands of floating robots called Argo floats has measured its temperature at depth since the early 2000s. Warm water expands, and melting glaciers add more, so sea level rises. Tide gauges and satellites agree that global sea level has risen about 20 centimeters since 1900, and the rate has roughly doubled in recent decades. The ocean has also absorbed about a quarter of our carbon dioxide, which has made it measurably more acidic, a change that stresses corals and shellfish.

Scientists distinguish between what is very certain and what is less so. That Earth has warmed, that human emissions are the main cause, and that more emissions mean more warming is settled beyond reasonable dispute. Exactly how much warming a given amount of carbon dioxide produces, how fast ice sheets will respond, and how rainfall will change in a particular region are areas of active research with real ranges of uncertainty. Good science states both the confidence and the range.

words.d: a long cylinder of ice drilled from a glacier or ice sheet whose layers record past climate and trapped ancient air
a natural archive such as tree rings, corals or sediments that stands in for direct measurements of past climate
the increase in the average height of the ocean surface, caused by warming water expanding and by melting land ice
the lowering of seawater pH as the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the air

look.title: Four Witnesses
look.text: Imagine a courtroom. The first witness is a thermometer record from weather stations. The second is a satellite that has watched Arctic ice shrink for 45 years. The third is a tide gauge in New York that has recorded the sea creeping up since the 1850s. The fourth is a farmer's diary noting that the last spring frost has moved earlier over her lifetime. None of them talked to each other.
look.prompt: Why is agreement among independent kinds of evidence more convincing than any one record alone? What would it take to explain them all away?

check.q: Roughly how much has Earth's average surface temperature risen since the late 1800s?
choices: About 10 degrees Celsius
About 5 degrees Celsius
A little over 1 degree Celsius
It has not changed measurably
check.why: Independent analyses by NASA, NOAA and others put the warming at slightly more than 1 degree Celsius, most of it since 1970.

check.q: Why do scientists trust the warming record more because NASA, NOAA and the UK Met Office analyze it separately?
choices: Because three agencies have more money
Because independent methods reaching the same result make an error in any one method unlikely
Because the agencies share one dataset
Because government agencies cannot be wrong
check.why: Independent replication is a core test in science; agreement across different methods rules out most mistakes.

check.q: Which of these is a matter of genuine ongoing scientific uncertainty?
choices: Whether Earth has warmed at all
Whether human emissions are the main cause
Whether carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation
How fast ice sheets will respond and how rainfall will change region by region
check.why: The basic facts of warming and its cause are settled; the pace of ice loss and regional rainfall changes carry real ranges of uncertainty.

lessons.title: What Models Can and Cannot Do
lessons.mainIdea: Climate models are physics run forward on computers; they cannot predict a given year's weather but have correctly projected the long-term warming trend.
reading: A *climate model* is a set of equations for how air and water move, how heat and moisture are exchanged, and how sunlight is absorbed and reflected, solved over a grid of boxes covering the planet. Weather forecasters use nearly the same equations to predict next week. Climate modelers run them for centuries. The difference is the question asked. A forecast asks what the sky will do on Tuesday. A climate projection asks what the average of many Tuesdays will be in 2070 if emissions follow a certain path. You cannot predict the next coin flip, but you can predict very well how many heads a thousand flips will give.

Models are tested against the past. Start one in 1850 with the observed changes in sunlight, volcanoes and greenhouse gases and it reproduces the measured warming, the cooling after big eruptions, and the faster warming in the Arctic. Run it without the human-added greenhouse gases and it fails to reproduce the warming since 1970. That is the main way scientists attribute recent warming to human activity: nothing else in the models can make the curve.

Models also made predictions that came true. Projections published in the 1970s and 1980s, from models far cruder than today's, forecast warming rates close to what was later measured. They predicted that the stratosphere would cool while the surface warmed, which is what greenhouse gases should do and what satellites later found. They predicted nights would warm faster than days and that the Arctic would warm fastest. Each confirmed prediction is a test the theory could have failed.

What models do worst is the local and the sudden. A global model's grid boxes are tens of kilometers wide, too coarse to capture a thunderstorm or a single city. Clouds are the biggest source of uncertainty, because whether warming makes more low clouds (cooling) or fewer (warming) is hard to simulate. That is the main reason estimates of *climate sensitivity*, the warming from doubling carbon dioxide, span a range of roughly 2.5 to 4 degrees Celsius rather than a single number. A range is not a failure. It is an honest statement of what is known, and the entire range means substantial warming.

words.d: a computer program that solves the physics of air, ocean, land and ice to simulate how climate responds to changes such as added greenhouse gases
a model's estimate of future climate under a stated set of assumptions, such as a particular path of emissions
the long-term global warming expected from doubling the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere
the scientific work of determining how much of an observed change is due to a particular cause, such as human emissions

look.title: The Two Runs
look.text: Picture two graphs from the same model. In the first, the model is fed everything that happened since 1850: the sun's small wobbles, each volcanic eruption, and the rising greenhouse gases from human activity. Its line tracks the measured global temperature closely, including the dips after eruptions. In the second, the human-added gases are removed and everything else is kept. The line stays flat after 1970 while the real measurements climb away from it.
look.prompt: What does the gap between the second run and the real record tell you? What would you want to check before trusting that conclusion?

check.q: Why can climate models project average conditions in 2070 when weather forecasts fail after two weeks?
choices: Climate models use better computers
Long-term averages are predictable even when individual days are not, like the count of heads in many coin flips
Weather is random but climate is not physics
Climate models ignore the atmosphere
check.why: Chaos limits day-by-day forecasts, but the statistical response of the whole system to added heat is far more predictable.

check.q: Which prediction made by early climate models was later confirmed by measurement?
choices: The stratosphere would warm along with the surface
The oceans would cool
The stratosphere would cool while the surface warmed
The Arctic would warm more slowly than the tropics
check.why: Greenhouse gases trap heat below, warming the surface and cooling the stratosphere, exactly as satellites later observed.

check.q: What is the largest source of uncertainty in estimates of climate sensitivity?
choices: Whether carbon dioxide absorbs heat
The size of the sun
The number of weather stations
How clouds will change as the planet warms
check.why: Cloud behavior is hard to simulate and can either add to or subtract from warming, which widens the range.

lessons.title: Impacts in the Midwest
lessons.mainIdea: For Illinois, climate change means more heavy downpours, hotter summers, shifting growing seasons and stress on rivers and lakes, with both costs and a few gains.
reading: Climate change is often pictured as melting glaciers and drowning islands, far from Illinois. But the Midwest has its own signature, and it is already measurable. Warmer air holds more water vapor, roughly 7 percent more for each degree Celsius of warming. When that air finally rises and cools, it rains harder. Records from Illinois weather stations show that the heaviest downpours, the kind that once came every few years, now come more often, and that total spring rainfall has risen. Chicago's combined sewer system, which carries rain and sewage in the same pipes, overflows into the river and, on the worst days, into basements and Lake Michigan.

Summers are getting hotter, though not evenly. Nights have warmed more than days, and humidity has risen, which matters for people and for livestock because humid heat is harder for bodies to shed. The 1995 Chicago heat wave killed more than 700 people in a week, most of them elderly residents in apartments without air conditioning. Heat is already the deadliest kind of weather in the United States, and models project many more days above 35 degrees Celsius in Illinois by late in the century.

For farms the picture is mixed. A longer frost-free season and more carbon dioxide can boost some crops, and Illinois growers now plant corn earlier than their grandparents did. But wetter springs delay planting and drown seedlings, hotter July nights reduce corn yields by making the plant burn energy instead of filling kernels, and heavy rains wash away soil and nitrogen. Pests and crop diseases that once died in winter now survive. On balance, most agricultural studies project that the gains fade and the losses grow as warming continues.

Lake Michigan tells a subtle story. Warmer winters mean less ice cover and more evaporation, yet heavier rains push levels up; the lake has swung between record lows in 2013 and near-record highs in 2020, eroding Chicago beaches and flooding lakefront paths. Rivers run higher in spring and lower in late summer. None of these changes ends life in Illinois. They add cost, risk and uncertainty to a place built around a climate that is no longer quite the one it was built for.

words.d: a sewer system that carries both stormwater and sewage in the same pipes and overflows untreated into rivers during heavy rain
a stretch of days with temperatures far above normal, dangerous especially when nights stay hot and air is humid
the frost-free part of the year when crops can grow
water in gas form in the air; warmer air can hold more of it, which fuels heavier rain

look.title: A Week in July
look.text: Picture Chicago in a projected July of 2070. Overnight lows stay above 27 degrees Celsius for six nights. A three-inch downpour hits on the fourth afternoon; the river reverses briefly into the lake, and viaducts flood. A farmer in Kankakee County reports her corn is tasseling early but the nights are too hot for good kernel set. A cooling center on the West Side is full.
look.prompt: Which of these effects trace back to the same physical cause? Which groups of people are hurt most, and what could a city do now to reduce that harm?

check.q: Why does a warmer climate produce heavier downpours?
choices: Storms move more slowly
Clouds are lower
There are more rivers to evaporate
Warmer air holds more water vapor, so more falls when it rains
check.why: Air holds about 7 percent more moisture per degree Celsius, so a storm in warmer air has more water to release.

check.q: What happens in Chicago's combined sewers during an extreme rainstorm?
choices: Sewage and stormwater overflow untreated into the river and sometimes the lake
The pipes store the water until it evaporates
Rain is diverted to farms
The system shuts off automatically
check.why: Because sewage and rain share the same pipes, heavy rain overwhelms treatment capacity and the mix is released.

check.q: Why do hotter July nights lower corn yields?
choices: Corn needs frost to ripen
The plant burns energy at night instead of storing it in kernels
Nights are when corn absorbs sunlight
Warm nights attract more birds
check.why: Plants respire at night; warmer nights raise that energy cost and leave less for filling grain.

lessons.title: Mitigation and Carbon Accounting
lessons.mainIdea: Reducing emissions starts with counting them honestly, source by source, and the biggest sources are electricity, transportation, industry and agriculture.
reading: *Mitigation* means reducing the cause: cutting the greenhouse gases we add to the air. The first step is counting. Governments, companies and cities keep *greenhouse gas inventories*, ledgers that tally emissions by source. For the United States, the largest slices are transportation and electricity generation, each roughly a quarter to a third, then industry, then buildings and agriculture. Agriculture's share comes mostly from methane, which cattle produce as they digest, and nitrous oxide, which soil bacteria release from fertilizer. Both are far stronger heat-trappers per molecule than carbon dioxide.

Different gases are compared using *carbon dioxide equivalent*: the amount of carbon dioxide that would trap the same heat over a hundred years. Methane counts about 28 times its weight; nitrous oxide about 265. This lets a farm, a factory or a country add up everything into one number and track it over time. Illinois's inventory shows the state's emissions have fallen since the mid-2000s, mainly because coal plants closed and were replaced by natural gas, wind and existing nuclear plants.

A carbon footprint is the same accounting applied to a person or a product. The average American's footprint is among the highest in the world, roughly 15 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent per year, several times the global average. Where it comes from matters more than the total: for most households, the big items are driving, flying, home heating and electricity, and beef. Recycling and reusable bags are good habits, but they move the number very little compared with those four.

Mitigation options are ranked by cost per ton avoided. Some, such as efficiency improvements in buildings and switching from coal to wind, pay for themselves. Others, such as capturing carbon from the air, remain expensive. The world's emissions are still rising, though more slowly, and the gap between what countries have pledged and what the physics requires is large. Carbon accounting does not close that gap. It shows exactly where it is.

words.d: actions that reduce the causes of climate change, mainly by cutting greenhouse gas emissions
an accounting of a country's, company's or city's emissions, listed by source and gas
a way to express the warming effect of any greenhouse gas as the amount of carbon dioxide that would trap the same heat
the total greenhouse gases caused by a person, product or activity, usually measured per year

look.title: Carbon per Kilowatt-Hour, Over a Plant's Whole Life
look.cite: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2014, median life-cycle estimates, rounded
look.prompt: These figures include building and fueling each plant, not just running it. Which switch cuts the most carbon per kilowatt-hour, and why is that switch not free?

check.q: Why is methane from cattle counted as more than its weight in a greenhouse gas inventory?
choices: Because cattle produce so much of it
Because methane traps far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide
Because it lasts longer than carbon dioxide
Because it is counted twice
check.why: Carbon dioxide equivalent scales each gas by its heat-trapping power; methane is about 28 times stronger over a century.

check.q: Which household change would reduce a typical American's carbon footprint the most?
choices: Driving and flying less and using less home energy
Switching to paper bags
Recycling more cans
Turning off lights in empty rooms
check.why: Transportation, home energy and beef dominate personal emissions; small habits matter far less by the numbers.

check.q: Illinois emissions have fallen since the mid-2000s mainly because
choices: the population decreased sharply
farms stopped using fertilizer
coal power plants closed and were replaced by gas, wind and nuclear
cars were banned in Chicago
check.why: Electricity generation shifted away from coal, the most carbon-intensive fuel, which lowered the state's inventory.

lessons.title: Adaptation
lessons.mainIdea: Because some warming is already locked in, communities must also adapt, redesigning buildings, farms and cities for the climate they will actually have.
reading: Even if the world stopped emitting tomorrow, the carbon dioxide already in the air would keep the planet warm for centuries. *Adaptation* means adjusting to changes that mitigation cannot prevent. It is not giving up; it is the other half of the job. A city that cuts its emissions and also builds a bigger storm sewer is doing both.

Chicago's Deep Tunnel is an adaptation project that began before anyone used the word. Since the 1970s the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District has bored more than 100 miles of tunnels hundreds of feet beneath the city, some 10 meters across. They hold stormwater until treatment plants can catch up. Giant reservoirs in old quarries hold billions of gallons more. The system was designed for the storms of the past century, and heavier rains now push it to its limits. So the city is adding green roofs, permeable pavement and rain gardens that soak water in where it falls.

Heat is the deadliest threat, and its adaptations are cheaper: trees. A shaded street can be 5 to 10 degrees Celsius cooler than a bare one on a hot afternoon. Mapping after the 1995 heat wave showed that deaths clustered in neighborhoods with few trees, more pavement and more isolated elderly people. Planting trees, painting roofs white, opening cooling centers and checking on neighbors are adaptation, and they save lives every summer. Farmers adapt too, with earlier planting, drought-tolerant seed, tile drains sized for bigger storms and cover crops that hold soil through a downpour.

Adaptation has limits. Sea walls protect a coast only up to the height they were built. A crop can tolerate only so much heat. And adaptation is unequal: wealthy places can afford tunnels and air conditioning; poor ones and poor countries often cannot, though they did least to cause the problem. Deciding who pays for adaptation, and how much warming to plan for, is a question science can inform but not answer alone.

words.d: adjusting buildings, farms, cities and habits to cope with climate changes that cannot be prevented
rain gardens, permeable pavement, green roofs and trees that manage stormwater and heat using natural processes
the tendency of a city, with its pavement and rooftops, to be hotter than the countryside around it, especially at night

look.title: Two Blocks in July
look.text: On one Chicago block, mature elms arch over the street, front yards are grass, and the roofs are light-colored. Four blocks away, the trees were cut for a road widening decades ago, the lots are paved for parking, and the roofs are black tar. On a 36-degree afternoon a thermometer on the second block reads several degrees higher, and at midnight the pavement is still radiating heat into the apartments above.
look.prompt: Which adaptations would make the biggest difference on the second block, and which are cheapest? Why might that block have fewer trees in the first place?

check.q: Why is adaptation necessary even if emissions are cut sharply?
choices: Because mitigation does not work
Because warming has already stopped
Because carbon dioxide already in the air will keep warming the planet for centuries
Because adaptation is cheaper than mitigation
check.why: Carbon dioxide lingers for hundreds of years, so some change is locked in regardless of future emissions.

check.q: What is the main purpose of Chicago's Deep Tunnel system?
choices: To supply drinking water
To carry trains under the river
To store stormwater during heavy rains until treatment plants can process it
To generate hydroelectric power
check.why: The tunnels and reservoirs hold combined sewage and stormwater that would otherwise overflow into the river and basements.

check.q: Why did deaths in the 1995 Chicago heat wave cluster in certain neighborhoods?
choices: Those areas had more trees
Those areas had fewer trees, more pavement and more isolated residents
Those areas were closer to the lake
Those areas had more air conditioning
check.why: Heat islands and social isolation made some neighborhoods far more dangerous, which points to trees and neighbor checks as adaptations.

lessons.title: Environmental Justice
lessons.mainIdea: Pollution and climate risk are not spread evenly; they fall hardest on low-income communities and communities of color, and environmental justice asks why and what to do about it.
reading: Hazel Johnson lived in Altgeld Gardens, a public housing development on Chicago's far South Side. She came to call the area a toxic doughnut: landfills, a sewage treatment plant, chemical factories and abandoned industrial sites on every side. Her husband died of lung cancer in 1969. She noticed how many neighbors had cancer, asthma and other illnesses, and she began going door to door with a survey. In 1979 she founded People for Community Recovery to fight for cleanup and for information about what was in the air, water and soil. She is often called the mother of the environmental justice movement.

*Environmental justice* is the principle that no group of people should bear a disproportionate share of environmental harms, and that everyone should have a voice in decisions that affect their environment. Study after study has found the same pattern Johnson saw: hazardous waste sites, highways, refineries and power plants are more likely to be located in low-income neighborhoods and in Black, Latino and Native communities. Sometimes the polluter came first and only cheap housing was left nearby. Often the neighborhood had the least political power to say no. Either way, residents breathe more particulate matter, live with more lead, and have higher asthma rates.

Flint, Michigan, showed how the pattern extends to water. In 2014 the city, under state-appointed emergency managers, switched its water source to the Flint River to save money and did not add the chemical that prevents pipes from corroding. Lead from old pipes leached into the tap water of a majority-Black city where much of the population was poor. Residents complained for more than a year before officials accepted the findings of outside scientists and a local pediatrician who showed that children's blood lead levels had risen. Lead causes permanent harm to developing brains. Chicago, which has more lead water service lines than any other American city, is replacing them slowly.

Climate change adds a layer. Heat waves kill in the neighborhoods with the fewest trees. Floods hit the low-lying areas where housing is cheapest. In 1994 the federal government directed agencies to consider environmental justice in their decisions, and Illinois now requires extra review and community notice for polluting facilities in already burdened areas. Science can map the burden. Deciding that the map is unacceptable is a choice a society makes.

words.d: the principle that environmental harms and benefits should be shared fairly and that affected people should have a say in decisions
out of proportion; a larger share than would be fair or expected
a lead pipe carrying water from the street main into a building, a major source of lead in tap water
adding chemicals to water so it does not dissolve metal from the pipes it flows through

look.title: A Federal Directive
look.text: Executive Order 12898, signed in February 1994, directed every federal agency to make achieving environmental justice part of its mission by identifying and addressing disproportionately high and adverse human health or environmental effects of its programs and policies on minority populations and low-income populations.
look.cite: Executive Order 12898, Federal Actions to Address Environmental Justice in Minority Populations and Low-Income Populations, 1994 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: This order asks agencies to identify and address unequal harms. What kinds of data would an agency need to collect to know whether a harm is disproportionate?

check.q: What did Hazel Johnson's door-to-door survey in Altgeld Gardens reveal?
choices: That the neighborhood had no pollution
That residents wanted more factories
That the area's air was cleaner than downtown
Unusually high rates of cancer, asthma and other illness in a neighborhood surrounded by polluting sites
check.why: Her survey documented a pattern of illness that matched the ring of landfills and factories around the development.

check.q: What caused lead to enter Flint's tap water in 2014?
choices: The city switched water sources without adding corrosion control, so lead leached from old pipes
The Flint River is naturally rich in lead
A factory dumped lead into the treatment plant
Residents installed new lead pipes
check.why: Corrosive river water without treatment dissolved lead from aging service lines into homes.

check.q: Which statement best describes the environmental justice pattern that research has found?
choices: Pollution is spread evenly across all neighborhoods
Polluting facilities are more often located near low-income communities and communities of color
Wealthy neighborhoods have the most landfills
Only rural areas face environmental harm
check.why: Studies consistently find that hazardous sites and heavy infrastructure cluster near communities with the least political power.

lessons.title: Policy Tools
lessons.mainIdea: Governments can reduce pollution by setting rules, putting a price on it, or creating tradable permits, and each tool has strengths the others lack.
reading: Suppose a state wants less sulfur dioxide from its power plants. The oldest tool is a *regulation*: a rule that says each smokestack may emit no more than a set amount, or must install a scrubber. Rules are clear and enforceable, and for something like lead in gasoline, where the goal is zero, they work best. Their weakness is that they treat every plant the same. A plant that could cut emissions cheaply has no reason to cut more than the rule demands, and a plant where cuts are very expensive must pay anyway.

A second tool is a *tax*: charge each ton of pollution. Now every plant has a reason to cut as much as it cheaply can, and the cheapest cuts happen first. Economists generally favor this because it gets the most reduction per dollar. Its weakness is that the total reduction is uncertain; you set the price and see what happens. Politically, taxes are hard to pass. A few places tax carbon; many more subsidize the alternatives instead, which is the tool the United States has mostly used for wind, solar and electric vehicles.

The third tool combines the two. In *cap and trade*, the government sets a total limit, the cap, and issues that many permits. Plants that cut cheaply can sell spare permits to plants that cannot. The total is guaranteed and the cheapest cuts still happen first. The 1990 Clean Air Act amendments used this for sulfur dioxide, and acid rain emissions fell faster and far more cheaply than industry had predicted. California and a group of northeastern states now run cap-and-trade markets for carbon dioxide. The risk is a cap set too loose, which makes permits nearly free and changes little.

Choosing a tool depends on the problem. Is the harm so severe that a hard limit is needed? Is the pollution easy to measure at the source? Are there many sources with very different costs? Are the public and lawmakers willing to see a price attached? Environmental science provides the first three answers; the fourth belongs to citizens, which is one reason to understand the tools well enough to argue about them.

words.d: a legally binding rule, such as a limit on emissions or a required technology
a policy that sets a total limit on pollution and lets companies buy and sell permits within that limit
a fee charged per ton of carbon dioxide emitted, meant to make polluting more expensive than cutting pollution
a government payment or tax break that makes a product or activity cheaper, such as credits for wind or solar power

look.title: Three Plants, One Goal
look.text: A state has three coal plants. Plant A can cut a ton of sulfur dioxide for 100 dollars, Plant B for 300 dollars and Plant C for 900 dollars. The state wants total emissions cut by 300 tons. A regulation orders each plant to cut 100 tons. A cap-and-trade system gives each plant permits and lets them trade.
look.prompt: Under the rule, what is the total cost of the 300-ton cut? Under trading, which plant will do the cutting and what happens to the total cost? Who might object to the trading result?

check.q: What is the main weakness of a one-size-fits-all emission rule?
choices: It cannot be enforced
It ignores that cutting pollution costs different amounts at different sources
It always sets the limit too high
It applies only to cars
check.why: A uniform rule forces expensive cuts at some plants while leaving cheap cuts undone at others.

check.q: In a cap-and-trade system, what is guaranteed?
choices: The price of a permit
That every plant cuts the same amount
The total amount of pollution allowed
That no plant pays anything
check.why: The cap fixes the total; trading lets the market decide who cuts and sets the permit price.

check.q: Which policy tool did the 1990 Clean Air Act amendments use to cut acid rain?
choices: A carbon tax
A ban on coal
Subsidies for scrubbers
A cap-and-trade market for sulfur dioxide permits
check.why: The acid rain program capped total sulfur dioxide and let plants trade permits, cutting emissions faster and cheaper than expected.

lessons.title: Costs, Benefits and Trade-offs
lessons.mainIdea: Every environmental decision trades one thing for another, and honest analysis puts numbers on both sides while admitting what cannot be priced.
reading: When the EPA proposes a new limit on soot, it must estimate what the rule will cost: scrubbers, fuel switches and higher electric bills. It must also estimate what the rule will gain: fewer hospital visits, fewer missed work days and fewer early deaths. This is *cost-benefit analysis*. Its retrospective studies of the Clean Air Act have found the health benefits outweighing the costs many times over. But the method requires assigning dollar values to things like a year of life or a clear view across the Grand Canyon, and reasonable people disagree about those numbers.

The heart of the problem is the *externality*: a cost that falls on someone who was not part of the deal. A coal plant sells electricity to its customers; the asthma downwind falls on people who bought nothing. Because the polluter does not pay that cost, it produces more pollution than it would if it did. Most environmental policy is an attempt to make the external cost internal, whether by rule, tax or permit, so the price of a thing reflects what it truly costs.

Trade-offs run in every direction. Cheaper electricity from coal means more mercury in fish. A wind farm displaces coal but kills some birds and bats and changes a landscape people love. Banning a pesticide protects streams but may raise food prices or push farmers to a worse chemical. Requiring corrosion control in Flint would have cost the city a few hundred dollars a day; skipping it cost hundreds of millions and a generation's health. Not every trade-off is close.

Two ideas help. *Risk assessment* asks how likely a harm is and how bad, so that a small chance of catastrophe is not weighed the same as a large chance of inconvenience. The precautionary principle says that when a harm could be severe and irreversible, lack of full certainty should not be a reason to delay action. Critics note that waiting for certainty is itself a choice with costs. The ozone case is the model: action came before the science was complete, the science firmed up, and the action was strengthened. Waiting would have been far more expensive.

words.d: comparing the total costs of a decision with its total benefits, usually in dollars, to judge whether it is worthwhile
a cost or benefit of an activity that falls on people who were not part of the transaction, such as pollution downwind of a factory
estimating how likely a harm is and how severe it would be, to guide decisions about it
the idea that when a possible harm is severe and irreversible, action should not wait for complete scientific certainty

look.title: Adding Up Clean Air
look.text: In its study of the Clean Air Act amendments, the EPA estimated that by 2020 the rules would prevent hundreds of thousands of premature deaths each year along with millions of cases of respiratory illness and lost work and school days, and that the dollar value of these benefits would exceed the costs of compliance by a wide margin, on the order of thirty to one under the agency's central estimate.
look.cite: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, The Benefits and Costs of the Clean Air Act from 1990 to 2020, 2011 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: A thirty-to-one ratio depends on how a prevented death is valued in dollars. What would change if that value were set much lower, and who should decide it?

check.q: What is an externality?
choices: A cost that falls on people outside the transaction, such as pollution downwind
The price of a product in another country
A tax on imports
The cost of building a factory
check.why: Externalities are costs or benefits not reflected in the price, which is why markets alone produce too much pollution.

check.q: Why do critics say cost-benefit analysis is hard to apply to environmental rules?
choices: Because costs are never measurable
Because it requires dollar values for things like health and scenery that people value differently
Because benefits always exceed costs
Because the EPA does not use it
check.why: Costs are usually clear; benefits like a life saved or a river restored must be converted to dollars, and that step is contested.

check.q: How does the ozone story illustrate the precautionary principle?
choices: Nations waited until the science was complete before acting
The problem solved itself
Action began before every detail was certain, and was strengthened as evidence grew
Scientists refused to recommend policy
check.why: The Montreal Protocol was signed when the mechanism was strong but not fully confirmed, then tightened as measurements came in.

lessons.title: Designing a Sustainable Community
lessons.mainIdea: A sustainable community is designed as a system, with energy, water, food, waste and transportation planned so the place can keep working for generations.
reading: *Sustainability* means meeting the needs of the present without using up the ability of future generations to meet theirs. That definition, from a 1987 United Nations report, sounds abstract until you apply it to a town. Where does its electricity come from, and will that source still be there in 50 years? Where does its water come from, and is the aquifer level falling? Where does its food come from, and is the soil holding? Where does its waste go? How do people get to work? A sustainable community is one where the honest answers to those questions do not point at a cliff.

The design tools are the ones this unit has built. Systems thinking maps the stocks and flows. Feedback loops show what will stabilize and what will run away. Life-cycle carbon accounting compares energy choices. Green infrastructure handles stormwater and heat. Walkable neighborhoods with transit cut the largest slice of a household's carbon footprint without asking anyone to give up going places. Buildings that are insulated and oriented to the sun use a fraction of the energy of ones that are not. Composting and recycling close material loops the way decomposers close them in a prairie.

Examples exist at every scale. Chicago's City Hall has grown a garden on its roof since 2000 to cool the building and soak up rain. A number of Illinois towns run on electricity from nearby wind farms. Communities from Copenhagen to Curitiba have built transit and bicycle networks that move most trips without cars. None of them is perfect, and each faced trade-offs: cost, space, the disruption of change, and the fact that people like the way things already are.

The last design principle is about who decides. Communities that planned with their residents, especially those in the most burdened neighborhoods, have generally built things that lasted. Environmental science supplies the evidence: the measurements, the mechanisms, the projections, the ranges. It cannot say how much a community should value a clean river against a lower tax bill, or the present against the future. Those are questions for citizens who understand the evidence well enough to argue from it. That, in the end, is why you learned this.

words.d: meeting present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet their own
adding up the environmental costs of a product or system from raw materials through use to disposal
describing a neighborhood where daily needs can be reached on foot or by transit rather than only by car
a system in which wastes become inputs, so little is thrown away, as in composting or a natural nutrient cycle

look.title: A Town on the Sangamon
look.text: A central Illinois town of 8,000 people gets electricity from the regional grid, water from the Mahomet Aquifer, and most of its jobs from farming and a grain elevator. Its downtown has emptied as stores moved to a highway strip. Heavy rains flood the same low neighborhood every few years. The town council has a modest budget and a survey showing residents want lower taxes, cleaner water and something done about flooding.
look.prompt: Using the tools from this unit, propose three changes the town could make. For each, name the stock or flow it affects, the trade-off it involves, and how you would know in ten years whether it worked.

check.q: Which definition of sustainability comes from the 1987 United Nations report?
choices: Using no resources at all
Growing the economy as fast as possible
Meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
Returning to pre-industrial life
check.why: The Brundtland definition centers on fairness between present and future generations.

check.q: Why does a walkable neighborhood with transit reduce a household's carbon footprint so much?
choices: Because walking produces no carbon dioxide at all
Because it replaces the largest slice, transportation, without requiring people to travel less
Because transit is free
Because it eliminates home heating
check.why: Driving is among the biggest personal emission sources; design that cuts car trips addresses it directly.

check.q: What role does environmental science play in a community's decisions, according to this lesson?
choices: It decides how much a community should value the future
It replaces the need for public debate
It sets tax rates
It supplies the evidence and projections that citizens then argue from
check.why: Science can measure and predict; weighing values and trade-offs remains a choice for the community.

review.q: A temperature inversion is dangerous for air quality because
choices: it causes acid rain
it destroys ozone
it traps pollution near the ground under a layer of warm air
it makes cars burn more fuel
review.why: With warm air aloft, smoke and exhaust cannot rise and disperse, as happened at Donora and London.

review.q: Which pollution source has the Clean Water Act had the least success controlling?
choices: Factory discharge pipes
Sewage treatment plants
Oil tankers
Nonpoint runoff from farms and streets
review.why: The law's permit system targets identifiable pipes; diffuse runoff has no pipe to regulate.

review.q: What evidence confirmed that chlorine from CFCs was destroying Antarctic ozone?
choices: Aircraft flights measured high chlorine monoxide exactly where ozone was lowest
Ozone levels rose after CFCs were introduced
The hole appeared only over factories
CFCs were found to be poisonous
review.why: The 1987 expeditions found the reactive chlorine compound right where ozone was being lost, matching the predicted mechanism.

review.q: The Keeling curve shows carbon dioxide rising from about 315 parts per million in 1958 to over 420 today. What do ice cores add to this record?
choices: Proof that volcanoes cause the rise
Evidence that before industry the level was about 280 and had not been this high in hundreds of thousands of years
Evidence that the level was higher in 1800
Nothing, since ice cores measure temperature only
review.why: Trapped air bubbles in ancient ice show pre-industrial levels near 280 ppm and no comparable level in 800,000 years.

review.q: How do scientists attribute recent warming mainly to human activity?
choices: By assuming the sun cannot change
By measuring warming only near cities
Models with natural factors alone fail to reproduce warming since 1970; adding human greenhouse gases matches the record
By counting the number of hot days
review.why: Attribution rests on running models with and without human emissions and comparing them to observations.

review.q: Which is an example of adaptation rather than mitigation?
choices: Replacing a coal plant with wind turbines
Taxing carbon dioxide emissions
Insulating a home to use less heating fuel
Planting street trees to cool a neighborhood during heat waves
review.why: Adaptation adjusts to warming that will happen; the other three reduce emissions.

review.q: What happened in Flint, Michigan, in 2014 that made it an environmental justice case?
choices: A cheaper, corrosive water source was used without treatment, and lead poisoned a poor, majority-Black city while complaints were ignored
A factory explosion released chlorine gas
The city banned lead pipes
A drought dried up the city's wells
review.why: The harm fell on a community with little political power, and officials dismissed residents' evidence for over a year.

review.q: In cap and trade, why do the cheapest pollution cuts happen first?
choices: Because the government orders the cheapest plants to cut
Because plants that can cut cheaply profit by selling spare permits to those that cannot
Because permits are free
Because all plants must cut equally
review.why: Trading lets plants with low costs cut extra and sell permits, so the total reduction is achieved at the lowest overall cost.
